teams.name: Buffalo Bills
analysis: The Jets gained 376 yards. They got twelve points out of them. That distinction keeps Buffalo first for us. The defense got off the field on ten of thirteen third downs, which let the Bills survive two giveaways and a 2-for-10 afternoon on third down themselves. James Cook's 74-yard run explains how an offense can skip that many steps. Against a defense that takes away the long run, we'd want more early touches for Dalton Kincaid. Buffalo has earned control of the AFC bye, but sustaining drives is how it keeps it.

mvp.stats: 2,223 pass yds · 13 pass TD · 7 INT · 290 rush yds · 11 rush TD
analysis: Two rushing touchdowns came out of a five-yard rushing afternoon. Allen's value to Buffalo lives in that contrast. Eleven rushing scores through nine games make it hard to put anybody else ahead of him.

mvp.name: Jared Goff
mvp.stats: 2,437 pass yds · 18 pass TD · 4 INT · 23 rush yds · 1 rush TD
analysis: Amon-Ra St. Brown needed just four catches for 98 yards and two scores, while Gibbs produced almost the same receiving yardage on seven. Goff can hand the defense two different assignment problems from one formation. Two interceptions in Germany keep us from treating 303 yards as a flawless performance. His season total of four picks puts the afternoon in perspective and keeps him fourth.

mvp.name: Jaxon Smith-Njigba
analysis: Drew Lock threw for 240 yards against Las Vegas. Smith-Njigba supplied 171 of them. A 71-yard gain will bend any box score, but the other seven catches still totaled a hundred. That is the strongest part of his case to us. Seattle can ask him for field position, an explosive finish and an answer for a different quarterback, all in the same game.

mvp.name: Patrick Mahomes
mvp.stats: 2,385 pass yds · 19 pass TD · 4 INT · 100 rush yds · 1 rush TD
analysis: Five touchdown throws on 35 attempts explain the score in Atlanta. What keeps Mahomes in the race is how little the defense gains by taking away the obvious target. Rashee Rice led Kansas City in receiving yards, yet the rookie back caught two scores. We'd still ask whether this offense can convert more third downs when the big play disappears. A seven-win start gives Mahomes time to answer.

mvp.name: Trevor Lawrence
mvp.stats: 2,284 pass yds · 21 pass TD · 5 INT · 106 rush yds · 0 rush TD
analysis: Lawrence hit Parker Washington for 152 yards and still had another 200 passing yards to distribute. That matters more to us than simply running up a total on Tennessee. Tilting coverage toward the first explosive target doesn't solve the rest of the field. Twenty-one passing scores against five interceptions keep his full-season case strong. His drop reflects the competition for places on this board.

mvp.name: Jahmyr Gibbs
mvp.stats: 41 rec · 384 rec yds · 2 rec TD · 1,000 rush yds · 11 rush TD
analysis: His 252 yards from scrimmage divided almost neatly into the jobs of a lead runner and a starting receiver. A carry can bring a safety forward on one series, and a catch can punish that same alignment on the next. We give Gibbs his own ballot spot alongside Goff because Detroit can change the question it asks a defense without changing the player who touches the ball.

mvp.name: Jordan Love
mvp.stats: 2,838 pass yds · 20 pass TD · 7 INT · 23 rush yds · 2 rush TD
analysis: Seventeen completions brought 220 yards against Minnesota. Green Bay still scored ten points because productive throws were interrupted by losses behind the line and four team giveaways. We separate Love's one interception from that team total. His season production keeps him on the board. For him to climb, we'd want more possessions where an early completion buys the offense an easier down and an actual scoring chance.

mvp.name: James Cook
mvp.stats: 12 rec · 110 rec yds · 0 rec TD · 971 rush yds · 9 rush TD
analysis: Even if you take the 74-yard run out of his afternoon, Cook gained 83 on his other seventeen carries. That is the argument for keeping him here despite the attention Allen commands near the goal line. Buffalo can ride the back for ordinary gains and still make a missed tackle cost an opponent most of the field. His 971 rushing yards make the run threat credible before Allen decides anything.

rookies.name: Sonny Styles
rookies.stats: 80 tackles · 1 sacks · 5 TFL · 4 passes defended · 1 INT
analysis: Thirteen tackles and one behind the line in a three-point division win pushed Styles to the top. New York still gained 399 yards, so we wouldn't use his tackle count as proof Washington controlled the game. What earns him first is the breadth of his season. He has interrupted passes, finished plays in the backfield and handled the volume of keeping an offense from turning a modest gain into an explosive one.

rookies.name: Arvell Reese
rookies.stats: 81 tackles · 4.5 sacks · 8 TFL · 4 passes defended · 1 INT
analysis: Styles and Reese each made thirteen tackles Thursday. What separates Reese's own case is the pressure production he brings in addition to that workload. Four and a half sacks and eight tackles for loss give New York a reason to send him forward even when his range is valuable behind the rush. We'd judge his next step by how often those negative plays leave the Giants in a third down they can close.

rookies.name: David Bailey
rookies.stats: 45 tackles · 7.5 sacks · 10 TFL · 3 passes defended · 0 INT
analysis: Last week's No. 1 broke up two passes against Buffalo even though he registered no sack and one tackle. That is a useful counterpoint to the idea that his whole value is whether the quarterback goes down. His 7.5 sacks and twelve quarterback hits remain the best argument for giving him first place again. We drop him two spots because Styles and Reese added more this week to already substantial season cases.

rookies.name: Jacob Rodriguez
rookies.stats: 80 tackles · 1 sacks · 4 TFL · 1 passes defended · 1 INT
analysis: One credited tackle against Indianapolis is a thin Sunday on which to base a promotion. We have Rodriguez fourth on the weight of eighty season tackles and the range of situations in which Miami needs him. The Colts getting 160 rushing yards from Taylor and McGowan also shows the limit of judging a linebacker by volume. We'd look for more stops behind the line before moving him into the top three.

rookies.name: Denzel Boston
analysis: A single 16-yard catch on two targets wasn't the engine of Cleveland's comeback. Fannin and Jeudy did more of the damage Sunday. Boston's season still gives him a specific place in the offense. His 523 yards on 33 catches yield almost sixteen per reception, enough to change field position without needing double-digit targets. We want to see him keep that threat while earning a steadier share of Watson's throws.

rookies.name: Caleb Downs
rookies.stats: 66 tackles · 2 sacks · 1 TFL · 3 passes defended · 1 INT
analysis: Eleven tackles against San Francisco meant plenty of work for the rookie safety. It also meant the ball reached his level far more often than Dallas wanted. We give him credit for the season's two sacks and interception alongside the tackle volume. That combination gives the staff a case for moving him closer to the action. The Cowboys first have to limit the explosives that make his depth indispensable.

rookies.name: Mansoor Delane
rookies.stats: 30 tackles · 0 sacks · 3 TFL · 7 passes defended · 1 INT
analysis: Atlanta reached the red zone five times and scored one touchdown. We can't assign the other four stops to a single defender, but Delane's two passes defended give us concrete evidence of his contribution on a difficult afternoon for Atlanta's receivers. Seven passes defended through this point and an interception make a stronger case than tackle volume for a corner. We keep him seventh.

rookies.name: KC Concepcion
rookies.stats: 40 rec · 458 rec yds · 1 rec TD · 43 rush yds · 1 rush TD
analysis: Cleveland targeted him eight times and got three catches for 21 yards. The more interesting contribution was the rushing touchdown. Giving a receiver a carry near scoring range makes the defense account for him even when Watson keeps the ball. Concepcion and Boston now have the same number of season targets and quite different uses. We moved Concepcion up for expanding the ways Cleveland can finish a drive.

rookies.name: Carnell Tate
analysis: Tate's receiving line stayed at 34 catches for 413 yards through the Jacksonville game. Tennessee needed more completions beyond the sticks, which is exactly where a receiver averaging over twelve yards a catch can help. We keep him on the board for the work already banked. For him to regain ground, the Titans need to turn his targets into a recurring answer for Ward on scoring drives.

rookies.name: Fernando Mendoza
rookies.stats: 191 pass yds · 0 pass TD · 0 INT · 25 rush yds · 1 rush TD
analysis: His first start came against Seattle, and he left it with a rushing touchdown and no interceptions. Seventeen completions on 29 attempts for 143 yards tell the other half. Las Vegas needed more from each successful throw just to keep drives affordable. We give him the last spot for protecting a close game while creating a score with his legs. Passing production under pressure will decide how long he holds it.

tiebreakers: Kansas City (3–1 in the West) edges Denver (2–1). Among the three 7–2 AFC division leaders, Kansas City owns the best conference mark at 6–1, ahead of Jacksonville (6–2) and Cincinnati (5–2). Jacksonville then wins the two-team comparison with Cincinnati on their head-to-head result. Denver opens the wild-card line despite matching all three in wins.

Detroit leads the NFC North on the record among the three tied teams. Detroit is 1–0, Minnesota 1–1 and Chicago 0–1. Once Detroit is placed, Minnesota’s win over Chicago gives the Vikings the first wild card. The Giants and Panthers hold home games as division leaders.

At 6–4, Seattle first represents the West ahead of the Rams on division record, 2–1 against 1–2. Green Bay then takes the final wild card over Seattle on conference record, 4–4 against 2–3. That order is why the Rams’ 4–2 NFC record doesn’t put them seventh.

Farther back, Las Vegas (3–3 in AFC games) leads Baltimore (2–5). The Chargers and Dolphins are each 1–5 in conference play, ahead of Tennessee at 1–6. Strength of victory gives Los Angeles the edge over Miami, .400 to .200. Tampa Bay leads New Orleans on division record, 2–0 to 0–2. Atlanta leads Arizona on conference record, 3–3 to 2–6.

highlights.team_of_week: Cincinnati • The Bengals gained 484 yards, held Pittsburgh to 222 and took first place in the AFC North. Burrow threw four scores without a pick. Chase didn’t need a touchdown to change the division.
highlights.biggest_risers: Cincinnati jumps six to No. 3. Washington climbs five to No. 21. Detroit, Minnesota and Indianapolis each gain four.
highlights.biggest_fallers: Denver and Miami each slide five. The Broncos sat while other contenders won. The Dolphins lost a two-point game to the Colts. Pittsburgh and Baltimore fall four apiece.
